intro: Justice in Scripture is not an abstraction. Mishpat is the verdict that protects the widow at the gate, and tsedaqah is the right relation that gives the orphan a place to belong. The prophets do not ask whether the church believes the right things about the poor. They ask what the church has done with its bread, its power, and its silence.

witnesses.name: Basil the Great
witnesses.role: Bishop who built a refuge for the sick and the destitute
witnesses.summary: Basil was a brilliant theologian who could have spent his life in scholarship and dispute. Instead he gave away his inheritance and built a complex on the edge of Caesarea, later called the Basileias, with a hospital, a hospice, and care for lepers no one else would touch. He preached that the bread in your cupboard belongs to the hungry and the coat in your closet belongs to the naked.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: He confronted the wealthy of his own city to their faces during a famine, organized food for the starving, and embraced lepers in public to break the fear that left them abandoned.
witnesses.honestNote: He could be sharp and imperious with rivals, and his fierce certainty in doctrinal fights sometimes hardened into a contempt for those who disagreed.

witnesses.name: William Wilberforce and the Clapham Sect
witnesses.role: Members of Parliament and reformers against the slave trade
witnesses.summary: Wilberforce was a gifted young politician whose conversion turned him toward the abolition of the British slave trade. Around him gathered the Clapham Sect, a circle of wealthy Christians who pooled their money, research, and influence over decades. They lost vote after vote and kept coming back.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: They fought for twenty years against a slave trade built into the economy of the empire, finally winning abolition in 1807 and emancipation in 1833, days before Wilberforce died.
witnesses.honestNote: Wilberforce was deeply conservative on other matters, opposing many labor protections for the English poor and at times defending the very order that kept them down.

witnesses.name: Hannah More
witnesses.role: Writer, educator, and ally of the abolitionists
witnesses.summary: More was a celebrated playwright and poet who left the fashionable world to give herself to the poor and to the abolition cause. She wrote the searing poem Slavery in 1788 and pamphlets that reached audiences the politicians never could. She opened Sunday schools across the Mendip villages where children had no other learning.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: She used her pen to put the cruelty of the slave trade in front of ordinary readers and built schools for the rural poor against the resistance of local landowners and farmers.
witnesses.honestNote: Her schools taught reading but withheld writing from poor children, since she feared educating them above their station, a limit she never fully outgrew.

witnesses.name: Lord Shaftesbury (Anthony Ashley Cooper)
witnesses.role: Aristocrat and parliamentary reformer for factory workers and children
witnesses.summary: Shaftesbury was an earl who spent his career fighting for people who had no vote and no voice. He drove the Factory Acts that limited brutal hours, the laws that pulled small children out of coal mines, and protections for boys sold as chimney sweeps. His faith was the engine of all of it.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: He pressed for laws against child labor in mines and mills and for the care of the mentally ill, often at the cost of standing against his own class.
witnesses.honestNote: He was rigid and suspicious of Roman Catholics and other groups, and his paternalism could treat the poor as objects of rescue rather than people with their own agency.

witnesses.name: Harriet Tubman
witnesses.role: Escaped slave who led others to freedom
witnesses.summary: Tubman escaped slavery and then went back, again and again, into the country that would have killed her. Guided by a faith she described in plain visionary terms, she led some seventy enslaved people north on the Underground Railroad and never lost one. During the Civil War she scouted and nursed for the Union army.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: She returned roughly thirteen times into slave territory to free family and strangers, carrying a pistol and trusting God, with a bounty on her head the whole time.
witnesses.honestNote: Her later years were marked by poverty and by a government that withheld the army pension she had earned, a cost she bore without becoming bitter, though she had every reason.

witnesses.name: Frederick Douglass
witnesses.place: Maryland and the northern United States
witnesses.summary: Douglass taught himself to read in defiance of the law, escaped slavery, and became the most powerful voice against it in America. His autobiography stripped the romance off the slaveholding South. He held the white church to account for blessing the chains.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: He spoke and wrote relentlessly for abolition and for the vote, distinguishing the slaveholding religion of the land from the Christianity of Christ, at real risk to his life and freedom.
witnesses.honestNote: He could be harsh and dismissive toward allies and rivals alike, and his disputes with other reformers sometimes turned personal in ways that wounded the cause.

witnesses.name: Sojourner Truth
witnesses.place: New York and the United States
witnesses.role: Preacher, abolitionist, and advocate for women
witnesses.summary: Born into slavery in New York as Isabella, she walked to freedom carrying her infant and then went to court to win back her son who had been sold illegally, one of the first Black women to win such a case against a white man. She took the name Sojourner Truth and traveled the country preaching, against slavery and for the dignity of women.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: She testified in churches and halls across a hostile country, won her son back through the courts, and worked to resettle freed people after the war.
witnesses.honestNote: She was unlettered and at times trusting of people who exploited her name and her labor, a vulnerability that followed her through much of her public life.

witnesses.name: William and Catherine Booth
witnesses.summary: The Booths left respectable ministry to take the gospel into the slums of East London, to the drunk, the prostitute, and the destitute the churches had given up on. Catherine preached as powerfully as William and insisted that women carry the same authority. They built soup kitchens, shelters, and rescue homes alongside the preaching.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: They organized food, housing, and rescue work for the poorest of London and campaigned against the exploitation of young girls, drawing mockery and violence from mobs and the press.
witnesses.honestNote: William ran the Army with an autocratic hand, and the rigid hierarchy he built bred control that sometimes crushed the very people closest to him.

witnesses.name: George Muller
witnesses.summary: Muller, a converted German who had once been a thief and a liar, opened homes that cared for more than ten thousand orphans over his lifetime. He refused on principle to ask anyone for money, choosing instead to pray and to record every answer. The orphanages of Ashley Down became famous for it.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: He took in destitute children no one else would and ran the homes for decades on prayer alone, never going into debt and never asking for funds.
witnesses.honestNote: His insistence that all giving be unsolicited could become a quiet pride in his own method, and his all consuming work left his own family at the margins of his attention.

witnesses.name: Charles Spurgeon
witnesses.role: Preacher who built an orphanage and cared for the poor
witnesses.summary: Spurgeon was the most famous preacher of Victorian London, but he refused to let his pulpit stay separate from the city outside it. He founded the Stockwell Orphanage for fatherless boys and later girls, a pastors college, and almshouses for the elderly poor. He gave away much of his own income.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: He raised and ran homes for orphans and the aged, trained poor men for ministry without charging them, and spoke against the slave trade when it cost him American readers.
witnesses.honestNote: He suffered from depression he sometimes hid behind certainty, and his combative public controversies could be ungenerous toward those he judged to have drifted from the truth.

witnesses.name: Amy Carmichael
witnesses.role: Missionary who rescued children from temple servitude
witnesses.summary: Carmichael went to South India and discovered young girls being given to temples and sold into ritual servitude and prostitution. She began taking them in, then boys as well, and built the Dohnavur Fellowship as a home for hundreds of rescued children. She stayed for fifty five years and never went home.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: She exposed and fought the temple trafficking of children, sheltering those she could reach despite legal danger and the fury of those who profited from the trade.
witnesses.honestNote: She ran Dohnavur with a controlling intensity, discouraged outside friendships for her workers, and her demand for total devotion could be smothering to those under her care.

witnesses.name: Martin Luther King Jr
witnesses.place: Atlanta, Montgomery, and the American South
witnesses.role: Pastor and leader of the civil rights movement
witnesses.summary: King was a Baptist preacher who put the prophets and the cross at the center of a movement against segregation. He led the Montgomery bus boycott, the march on Washington, and the campaigns in Birmingham and Selma that broke the legal back of Jim Crow. He paid for it with jail, threats, and finally his life.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: He pressed the nation toward the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act through nonviolent resistance, and at the end turned toward poverty and war at the cost of much of his support.
witnesses.honestNote: He was unfaithful to his wife and drew on the words of others without credit in his academic work, failings he never publicly reckoned with.

witnesses.name: John Perkins
witnesses.role: Pastor and founder of Christian community development
witnesses.summary: Perkins fled Mississippi after his brother was killed by a deputy, then chose to return to the place of his pain to preach the gospel and rebuild Black communities the system had stripped. He was beaten and tortured by police in a Brandon jail and came out preaching reconciliation rather than revenge. He built cooperatives, health centers, and a model of development led by the poor themselves.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: He joined the gospel to racial and economic justice on the ground in Mississippi, organizing the poor and confronting white churches that had blessed segregation.
witnesses.honestNote: He has said himself that his fierce drive cost his family dearly, with his children carrying the weight of a father given almost wholly to the work.

witnesses.name: Mother Teresa
witnesses.role: Founder of the Missionaries of Charity
witnesses.summary: She left a comfortable teaching post to live among the poorest in Calcutta and to gather the dying off the streets so they would not die alone. The order she founded spread to homes for the destitute, the sick, and the abandoned around the world. She did it while privately enduring decades of spiritual darkness in which she felt no presence of God.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: She and her sisters carried the dying, the leprous, and the unwanted into shelter and washed them, giving dignity to people the city had stepped over.
witnesses.honestNote: Her homes have been faulted for poor medical care and weak record keeping, and her readiness to accept money from corrupt donors drew fair criticism.

witnesses.name: Gary Haugen
witnesses.place: United States and the developing world
witnesses.summary: Haugen was a Department of Justice lawyer who led the United Nations investigation into the Rwandan genocide and came home convinced that the poor suffer most from a simple lack of protection. He founded International Justice Mission to put lawyers and investigators on the ground against slavery, trafficking, and police abuse. The work is unglamorous and slow.
witnesses.whatTheyDid: He built an organization that rescues people from forced labor and sexual slavery and works to make broken local justice systems actually protect the poor.
witnesses.honestNote: The rescue model has been questioned for relying on the same fragile and sometimes corrupt police forces it aims to reform, a tension Haugen has not fully resolved.
